findings.claim: All 42 practice questions across the seven lessons are labelled '40 marks — Shakespeare Essay'.
findings.truth: The novella is the 19th-century prose text in the modern and literary heritage component. Shakespeare sits in the other component. The label should read '40 marks — 19th-century prose essay'.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md, forms of assessment: Section B of the modern and literary heritage paper is 19th century prose, 40 marks; Shakespeare is Section B of the poetry paper.

findings.claim: All 42 mark ladders use non-house band names ('Top band (34–40)' with 'Lower bands', 'Band 6', or 'Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging') and none scales to the real 40-mark total.
findings.truth: Rescaled to five equal house bands: Top band (33-40), Upper-mid band (25-32), Mid band (17-24), Lower-mid band (9-16), Low band (1-8). Authored indicative content is kept where it existed.
findings.evidence: House ladder rule; 40 marks per question confirmed by the spec.

findings.claim: 'For OCR context questions, always connect Victorian social pressures to Stevenson’s methods.'
findings.truth: OCR sets one extended response on the novella. There is no separate context question, so the tip should speak about bringing context into any answer.
findings.evidence: spec: one extended response-style question from a choice of two.

findings.claim: 'Bye Street' is used as the name of the street with the door (description, content, a practice question and two knowledge-check items).
findings.truth: Stevenson never names the street. It is 'a by-street in a busy quarter of London' — a common noun for a side street.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 1: 'their way led them down a by-street in a busy quarter of London'.

findings.claim: 'Utterson says: “God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic, shall we say?… he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t specify the point.”'
findings.truth: Two speeches by two speakers were spliced. 'Troglodytic' is Utterson in ch. 2. 'A strong feeling of deformity' is Enfield in ch. 1.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 1: '“He is not easy to describe… he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t specify the point.”' (Enfield); ch. 2: 'said the perplexed gentleman… the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic'.

findings.claim: 'a “small man” who “trampled calmly”… gave him “a look so ugly it brought out the sweat on me like running.”'
findings.truth: Ch. 1 reads 'a little man' and 'gave me one look, so ugly that it brought out the sweat on me like running'. The flashcard carries the same loose wording.

findings.claim: Carew is 'an “aged” gentleman with “silvery hair”'; the flashcard repeats 'silvery hair'.
findings.truth: Ch. 4 reads 'an aged beautiful gentleman with white hair'. 'Silvery-haired' in the novella belongs to the old woman at Hyde’s Soho house.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg ch. 4 line 692 ('white hair') and line 787 ('An ivory-faced and silvery-haired old woman').

findings.claim: Carew is '“trampled” and “clubbed… with ape-like fury”'; the flashcard answer is "'Clubbed... with ape-like fury.'"
findings.truth: The splice does not exist. Hyde 'clubbed him to the earth. And next moment, with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim under foot'. The simile belongs to the trampling.

findings.claim: 'Stevenson puns on Utterson’s name (“he will be Mr Seek”) and on Hyde’s (“to hide”).'
findings.truth: The pun is on Hyde / hide, and the line reads 'If he be Mr. Hyde… I shall be Mr. Seek.'

findings.claim: 'Stevenson was writing in 1886, the year after W. T. Stead’s “Maiden Tribute” exposé…'
findings.truth: Stevenson wrote the novella in 1885 and Longmans published it on 5 January 1886. The exposé ran in July 1885, so he was writing in the same year.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde: first published 5 January 1886, Longmans, Green & Co.

findings.claim: Jekyll is '“deadly sick”'.
findings.truth: Ch. 5 reads 'looking deathly sick'.

findings.claim: Lanyon has '“a death warrant written legibly upon his face… he had his death-warrant written there.”'
findings.truth: The line appears once: 'He had his death-warrant written legibly upon his face.' The second half of the quotation was invented.

findings.claim: 'Lanyon is “hide-bound”, sticking to “the practical side of medicine”.'
findings.truth: 'The practical side of medicine' is not in the novella. Jekyll calls Lanyon 'that hide-bound pedant' in ch. 3, and Jekyll’s letter in ch. 9 says Lanyon is 'bound to the most narrow and material views'.

findings.claim: 1880s psychology 'including those of William James and early Freud' questioned the unity of the self.
findings.truth: Freud had published nothing on the unconscious in the 1880s; his theories come in the 1890s. The novella anticipates them. The flashcard repeats the claim.
findings.evidence: Freud’s Studies on Hysteria is 1895; the novella is 1886.

findings.claim: 'Poole… arrives at Utterson’s in “white and shaky” terror'; the flashcard repeats it.
findings.truth: 'White and shaky' is not in the novella. At Utterson’s, Poole says 'Mr. Utterson, sir, I’m afraid' and leaves his wine untasted; the white face comes later, in the square.

findings.claim: 'Poole notices three pieces of evidence: the voice sounds wrong, the hand glimpsed on the stair is ‘dwarfish’ and ‘hairy’, and a servant girl saw a creature ‘crying out like a rat’.'
findings.truth: Poole is the witness, not a servant girl. There is no hand on the stair. His evidence is the changed voice, the masked figure that was 'more of a dwarf' where his master is 'a tall, fine build of a man', and the cry 'like a rat'. 'Hairy' is Jekyll’s own hand in ch. 10.

findings.claim: Printed extract: '“The letter is a forgery,” said the lawyer, “the man has forged it.”'
findings.truth: Fabricated. Ch. 5 ends with Utterson’s thought: '“What!” he thought. “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer!” And his blood ran cold in his veins.' Guest only reports that the two hands are identical apart from the slope.

findings.claim: 'Jekyll’s “powers seemed shaken”, the drug stops working reliably…'
findings.truth: The quotation is invented and reverses the sense. Ch. 10 reads 'The powers of Hyde seemed to have grown with the sickliness of Jekyll.'

findings.claim: 'a drug that “could cast off the lower elements” of his personality'
findings.truth: The splice does not exist, and it inverts the mechanism. The drug substitutes 'a second form and countenance' that bears the stamp of 'lower elements in my soul'.

findings.claim: Lanyon: 'I cannot, even in my own thoughts, dwell on it without a start of horror.'
findings.truth: Ch. 9 reads 'I cannot, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror.'

findings.claim: 'Stevenson himself called the book ‘a fable’'; the flashcard asks for that 'genre label'.
findings.truth: The recorded self-description is 'a fine bogey tale', from Lloyd Osbourne’s account of Stevenson waking from the dream. 'A fable' is not traced to Stevenson.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde: '“Why did you wake me? I was dreaming a fine bogey tale.”'

findings.claim: Utterson is '“lean, cold, scanty, and yet somehow lovable.”'; the flashcard repeats it.
findings.truth: Ch. 1 reads 'lean, long, dusty, dreary and yet somehow lovable'. 'Cold, scanty' comes from an earlier clause about his discourse.

findings.claim: 'The front faces a respectable square: “a certain sinister block of building” with “a great air of wealth and comfort.”'
findings.truth: The two faces are swapped. 'A certain sinister block of building' is the back, on the by-street. The front on the square is the door that 'wore a great air of wealth and comfort'.

findings.claim: 'the laboratory is described as a “dismal” former dissecting theatre'
findings.truth: 'Dismal' describes the quarter of Soho in ch. 4. The laboratory is 'the dingy, windowless structure'.

findings.claim: 'When Utterson walks through London at night, “the fog settled down upon that part, as brown as umber”'
findings.truth: The scene is 'about nine in the morning, and the first fog of the season', in a cab to Soho, and the text reads 'settled down again upon that part'.

findings.claim: 'What are the three assessment objectives tested in Section B?' with 'AO1, AO2, and AO3' marked correct.
findings.truth: Four objectives are assessed on the 19th-century prose question: AO4 (spelling and punctuation) is assessed in Section B of each component. The true option was being marked wrong, and the stem also carried a banned section code.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md, assessment of extended responses: 'accurate spelling and punctuation (AO4) in Section B of each examined component'.

findings.claim: 'Your 19th-century novel question may offer a choice between an extract-based task and a discursive task, both assessing AO1, AO2 and AO3.'
findings.truth: The choice of two is fixed, not optional, and AO4 is assessed here as well.
findings.evidence: spec: 'one extended response-style question… from a choice of two' plus the AO4 rule above.

findings.claim: 'Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format, mark weightings and timing.'
findings.truth: The unit never states the real figures. The question is 40 marks, about an hour, closed text.
findings.evidence: spec: closed text, 2 hour paper, 80 marks, 40 for each section.

findings.claim: 'OCR marks AO1, AO2, and AO3 holistically' (and the same omission in the 'holistic marking' glossary entry).
findings.truth: Spelling and punctuation also carry marks on this question. No per-objective mark split is stated anywhere, because the spec publishes none.
findings.evidence: spec, assessment of extended responses (AO4 in Section B).

findings.claim: Flashcard answer "'Duplicity.'" for the question 'Which Jekyll word captures his strategy of secret indulgence?'
findings.truth: A one-word answer is only allowed when the question opens with What is / Who was / When / Name.

findings.claim: Utterson is called 'the novella’s primary narrator' (L5), and L6 teaches 'three narrators' and counts them in a knowledge check, while also saying the last chapter 'shifts from third-person mystery to first-person confession'.
findings.truth: Chapters 1-8 are third-person narration focalised through Utterson; only chapters 9 and 10 are first-person. Two options: (a) leave the shorthand, which is common teaching usage and consistent across L5-L6; or (b) change L5 to 'the eyes through which we see most of the story' and reword the L6 narrator count. Option (b) touches a knowledge check, a key fact and a glossary entry, so it needs a ruling. Recommendation: take option (b) only if the fleet is standardising this wording, otherwise leave. ORCHESTRATOR: "three narrative voices" is standard GCSE shorthand (Utterson-focused third person, Lanyon, Jekyll); left as is.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg: chapters 1-8 third person; ch. 9 'DR. LANYON’S NARRATIVE' and ch. 10 first person.

summary: Every lesson carried at least one error. The board layer was wrong across the whole unit: 42 practice questions were labelled Shakespeare essays and all 42 mark ladders used non-house band names that did not scale to 40 marks. Lesson 7 denied AO4, including a knowledge check that marked the true answer wrong. Thirteen quotations were misquoted, spliced or invented, including Utterson's description, Carew's white hair, Poole's evidence in chapter 8 and a fabricated printed extract in a lesson 3 practice question.
